strengths: Novel mechanistic interpretability contribution: introduces a Typographic Attention Score to localize a sparse set of specialized attention heads causally responsible for transmitting typographic information to the cls token in CLIP.

Provides genuine causal evidence (not just correlational) via the alpha-attention-manipulation experiment showing that suppressing spatial attention of circuit heads monotonically reduces typographic attack success.
Training-free method that scales to billion-parameter CLIP models (ViT-B through ViT-BigG) on consumer hardware, which is a practical advantage over gradient-based finetuning defenses.

Broad empirical validation across five model scales and multiple real-world typographic attack benchmarks (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT-DS) plus a synthetic ImageNet-100-Typo, alongside non-typographic benchmarks (ImageNet-100, Food-101, Aircraft) to check for capability preservation.
Reasonably transparent comparison to a finetuning baseline (Defense-Prefix), honestly reporting that the baseline outperforms on typographic robustness while framing the tradeoff on generalization.
Useful auxiliary analyses (intrinsic dimensionality across layers, attention-sink behavior of typographic heads) that support and enrich the main mechanistic claims.
Reasonable reproducibility details (hardware, hyperparameters, libraries used) and stated intent to release model weights.
weaknesses: The method is only compared against one baseline (Defense-Prefix); other cited defenses (projection-matrix method, SAE-based steering) are not empirically compared, limiting the strength of the competitive claims.

On the head-to-head comparison (Table 4), the training-free method is consistently outperformed by the finetuned baseline on typographic robustness itself, undermining the core claim of being 'competitive' with SOTA finetuning defenses.

The paper motivates the work heavily with VLM jailbreaks and malicious content generation (Fig. 1, intro), but all experiments are limited to CLIP zero-shot classification; no evaluation is done on actual VLM jailbreak or generation tasks, leaving the central motivating threat model untested.

The authors themselves acknowledge that the defense only protects the cls token, while many real applications (LLaVA, IP-Adapters) rely on spatial tokens where typographic information can still propagate — a significant limitation that is not empirically explored, only mentioned as future work.

The circuit construction and thresholding (epsilon, greedy head selection by ranked score) is somewhat heuristic; no ablation is shown for how sensitive the resulting robustness/accuracy tradeoff is to these design choices (e.g., different epsilon values, different ranking dataset).

The Typographic Attention Score is derived from a synthetic dataset (Unsplash-Typo) with a fixed, single text position (bottom center), raising questions about generalization to different attack placements/styles, though this is partially mitigated by testing on real-world datasets.
Appendix B's attention-sink explanation is based on a single head case study (H5,6 in ViT-B) and is largely anecdotal/exploratory rather than rigorously validated across heads or models.
Writing quality issues (e.g., 'behaivor', 'casual' instead of 'causal', inconsistent 'dyslexic'/'dislexic' spelling, grammatical errors) suggest the manuscript needs more careful proofreading.

The ablation-only intervention is coarse (binary head removal); no comparison to more graded or learned interventions is provided to assess whether finer control could yield a better robustness/accuracy tradeoff.

strengths: Presents a novel, well-motivated mechanistic interpretability analysis showing that typographic understanding in CLIP emerges abruptly in the second half of the model via a small set of specialized attention heads, supported by linear probing, attention-score analysis, and causal attention-manipulation experiments (varying alpha).

The proposed Dyslexify method is gradient-free, computationally cheap, and scales to billion-parameter models on modest hardware, which is a practical advantage over fine-tuning-based defenses like Defense-Prefix.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five OpenCLIP model scales (ViT-B to BigG), multiple typographic attack benchmarks (real and synthetic), and multiple non-typographic benchmarks, showing consistent robustness gains with minimal clean-accuracy loss.

Interesting and relevant application to a safety-critical medical foundation model (WhyLesionCLIP), demonstrating real-world impact of typographic attacks and the mitigation ability of the proposed method.

Thorough appendix with many supporting analyses (intrinsic dimensionality, attention-sink behavior, OCR degradation, runtime/memory comparisons, and an OCR+blur baseline), reflecting good scientific rigor and transparency, including reporting a baseline that outperforms their own method.
weaknesses: The simple OCR+blur baseline (Appendix J) consistently outperforms Dyslexify on the main ImageNet-100-Typo robustness benchmark across all model sizes, which somewhat undercuts the central claim that mechanistic circuit ablation is a strong practical defense; this important result is relegated to the appendix rather than being prominently discussed and contextualized in the main paper.

Despite motivating the work heavily with VLM jailbreaks and malicious generation from typographic attacks, the paper only evaluates zero-shot classification robustness; no experiments demonstrate that Dyslexify mitigates jailbreaks or malicious generation in actual VLM/downstream pipelines, leaving the central motivating threat model unaddressed.

Dyslexify only ablates contributions to the cls token, leaving spatial token representations (which are what downstream VLMs like LLaVA actually use) untouched — a significant limitation for the paper's own motivating use cases, acknowledged only briefly as future work.

No evaluation against adaptive attacks is performed; while the authors argue typographic attacks are non-differentiable, this leaves open whether an attacker aware of the ablated circuit could still craft effective attacks (e.g., via the α-manipulation experiments themselves suggesting a plausible adaptive strategy).

OCR capability is substantially degraded (8-30 percentage points depending on model/lexicon), which is a real practical cost of the method not thoroughly discussed or quantified against alternative partial-ablation strategies in the main text.

The circuit-construction procedure requires access to a typographic-labeled validation dataset per target model/domain (e.g., separate construction for ImageNet-100 vs. ISIC), which somewhat limits the plug-and-play generality suggested by the abstract.
Threshold choices (e.g., μ(T)+2σ(T) for head selection, ϵ=0.01 tolerance, k=10 max skips) appear heuristic without sensitivity analysis or principled justification.
